WebAssembly 32-bit, the instruction set of the `wasm32` targets (spec 07, section 6): the
instructions of its stack machine with what each pops and pushes, as the toolchain's backend
encodes them. They are declared in `arithmetic`, `compare`, `control`, `convert`, `local` and
`memory`; `vun-isa-wasm32`'s tables are generated from these declarations.
A block of wasm is the body of a function written as the text format has it, with Vun values
bound to the function's locals: `local_get(in(a))` pushes the value of `a`, `local_set(out(r))`
pops into the place `r`, and an instruction between them takes the stack as it stands. A
register of the table is a local, and its class the value type it holds. A block starts and ends
with an empty stack and has no branches.
A form's base is its opcode: the prefix byte (`0xfc` for the saturating conversions and the bulk

prefix, in the low bits.

doc: Atomic accesses of integers wider than an address, for a processor whose atomic instructions
reach one word (`lang.lower.soft`): on Thumb, where Arm's A profile has exclusive loads and
stores of two words (`lang.arch.thumb.Feature.application`), loops of them between barriers,
as the word's are made, which makes each sequentially consistent whatever order it asks. No
other processor has one written yet, and reaching one there is an error while compiling.

items.name: load
items.signature: load := unsafe ($T: type, p: *T, order: lang.mem.Order) -> T { $if _paired(T) { at := lang.mem.address(T, p); mut (low, high): (u32, u32) = (0, 0); unsafe lang.arch.asm({ ..lang.arch.thumb.names; dmb(sy); ldrexd(out(low).at(r2), out(high).at(r3), mem(in(at).at(r0))); dmb(sy); }); _joined(T, low, high) } else { $lang.diag.error(.{ .msg = _unsupported }) } }

items.name: store
items.signature: store := unsafe ($T: type, p: *T, value: T, order: lang.mem.Order) { $if _paired(T) { at := lang.mem.address(T, p); (low, high) := _words(T, value); unsafe lang.arch.asm({ ..lang.arch.thumb.names; push(r4, r5); dmb(sy); again := here(); ldrexd(r4, r5, mem(in(at).at(r0))); strexd(r1, in(low).at(r2), in(high).at(r3), mem(r0)); cmp(r1, 0); b(ne, again); dmb(sy); pop(r4, r5); }); } else { $lang.diag.error(.{ .msg = _unsupported }); } }

items.name: swap
items.signature: swap := unsafe ($T: type, p: *T, value: T, order: lang.mem.Order) -> T { $if _paired(T) { at := lang.mem.address(T, p); (low, high) := _words(T, value); mut (old_low, old_high): (u32, u32) = (0, 0); unsafe lang.arch.asm({ ..lang.arch.thumb.names; push(r4, r5); dmb(sy); again := here(); ldrexd(r4, r5, mem(in(at).at(r0))); strexd(r1, in(low).at(r2), in(high).at(r3), mem(r0)); cmp(r1, 0); b(ne, again); dmb(sy); mov(out(old_low).at(r0), r4); mov(out(old_high).at(r1), r5); pop(r4, r5); }); _joined(T, old_low, old_high) } else { $lang.diag.error(.{ .msg = _unsupported }) } }

items.name: compare_swap
items.signature: compare_swap := unsafe ($T: type, p: *T, expected: T, new: T, order: lang.mem.Order) -> T { $if _paired(T) { at := lang.mem.address(T, p); (low, high) := _words(T, expected); (new_low, new_high) := _words(T, new); wanted: [2]u32 = [new_low, new_high]; from := lang.mem.address([2]u32, lang.mem.pointer_to([2]u32, &wanted)); mut (old_low, old_high): (u32, u32) = (0, 0); unsafe lang.arch.asm({ ..lang.arch.thumb.names; done := label(); push(r4, r5, r6, r8); ldrd(r6, r8, mem(in(from).at(r1))); dmb(sy); again := here(); ldrexd(r4, r5, mem(in(at).at(r0))); cmp(r4, in(low).at(r2)); b(ne, done); cmp(r5, in(high).at(r3)); b(ne, done); strexd(r1, r6, r8, mem(r0)); cmp(r1, 0); b(ne, again); place(done); dmb(sy); mov(out(old_low).at(r0), r4); mov(out(old_high).at(r1), r5); pop(r4, r5, r6, r8); }); _joined(T, old_low, old_high) } else { $lang.diag.error(.{ .msg = _unsupported }) } }
doc: Stores `new` when `p` holds `expected`, giving what it held.

items.name: add
items.signature: add := unsafe ($T: type, p: *T, value: T, order: lang.mem.Order) -> T { $if _paired(T) { at := lang.mem.address(T, p); (low, high) := _words(T, value); mut (old_low, old_high): (u32, u32) = (0, 0); unsafe lang.arch.asm({ ..lang.arch.thumb.names; push(r4, r5, r6, r8); dmb(sy); again := here(); ldrexd(r4, r5, mem(in(at).at(r0))); adds(r6, r4, in(low).at(r2)); adc(r8, r5, in(high).at(r3)); strexd(r1, r6, r8, mem(r0)); cmp(r1, 0); b(ne, again); dmb(sy); mov(out(old_low).at(r0), r4); mov(out(old_high).at(r1), r5); pop(r4, r5, r6, r8); }); _joined(T, old_low, old_high) } else { $lang.diag.error(.{ .msg = _unsupported }) } }

items.name: sub

The grammar of Vun, defined once with `nodes.vun`, which holds the kinds of nodes and their
productions, and `tables.vun`, the tables that say how they nest: its tokens and tables. Generates the Rust `vun-grammar` crate, `lang.syntax`, the
formatter's tables and the editor grammars (spec 13, section 5).
`cargo gen` reads both files as literal data. Into Rust it translates each declaration by shape,
never by name:
- a `PascalCase` record of lists defines a kind: its entries are the kind's variants, and each
list is also a table of its own. An entry is `.name`, a spelling `"text"` (named after
itself), `.{ .name = .x, .text = "..." }`, or `.name(terms...)` for a kind with a production
(see `NodeKind`), whose fields and their counts, variants of `Count`, it derives;
- an `enum` declaration defines an enum;
- any other list is a table; `.name` items resolve to the one kind or enum that has them all.
What it interprets, the productions and the tables editors and the parser share (`parts`,
`admits`, `precedence`, ...), it reads by type, and resolves every name and path in them; what
editors make of the grammar is in `editors.vun`.

doc: Kinds of syntax tree nodes (spec 13, section 2), each with its production: the tokens and
children it spells, in source order.
A term of a production is a token spelled `"text"` (a punctuation or keyword token, or a name
spelled so where the grammar makes it a word), `.token(...)` for a token of one of the kinds
listed, each `.kind` or a path to a list of the token kind or a table of tokens,
`.word(path)` for a name or keyword spelled as a variant of the kind, or the list of one, the
path names, a child `.field`, `.optional(...)` and `.many(...)` for terms written once or not
and any number of times, `.separated(term, "sep")` for any number of `term` with `sep` between
them and after the last if written, `.choice(a, ...)` for one of the terms,
`.of(.field, table)` for a child in `field` of a kind the table lists,
`.starting(.field, tokens)` for one starting with a token a table of tokens lists, and
`.seq(...)` for terms in sequence. Tables are named by paths, as `grammar.infix`. Where a table
names kinds (`.of`, `holds`), a `transparent` node stands for the node it ends with, and its
last child stands where it stands, taking what that position takes.
A node is anchored at the first token of its production; its other tokens are `punct` leaves,
its children fill its fields. A field's count follows from where it stands: `many` in `many` or
`separated`, else `optional` in `optional` or `choice`, else `one`. A field named after a kind
holds a node of that kind, any other field any node. A leaf spells one token and holds nothing;
`punct` holds the token its parent's production names, `skipped` a token no production reads,
and neither stands in a field. An `error` stands for a child absent, or not one its position
takes, which it holds, and fits any field; an `error`, a `skipped` token, and a node holding
one or anchored at an absent token, are recovery's shapes: they fit their kind's fields, not
its production.

Shadow memory for the checks of unsafe code at run time (spec 07, section 7; spec 13,
section 8.7): one byte for each `granule` bytes of the address space, 0 where all of them
may be accessed, `k` where the first `k` may, and a negative code saying why where none may.
The shadow of each span of `1 << span_bits` addresses is reserved the first time memory in
it is described, so it follows the program's memory wherever the system puts it. A runtime
gives how memory is mapped (`mapped`) and exports the operations of `lang.check` over the
state (`exports`). The state is read and written by atomic accesses, which no check rewrites.

a stack of its own and never gives it back.

Deterministic simulation (spec 11, section 4): a test whose one parameter is `&mut Sim` runs
tasks, `std.task.Async` frames, on a virtual clock, one at a time, each next one chosen among
those ready by the case's choices. They are the choices a property's arguments are read from,
so a simulation runs over the cases a property does, a failing one is shrunk on its choices,
and `--seed` replays it exactly. Time passes only when no task is ready: the clock jumps to the
earliest time a task sleeps until.

items.name: Clock
doc: The clock of a simulation: virtual time, which tasks sleep on and which moves only when none
is ready. Shared by the tasks, which borrow it, and the simulation running them.

members.name: init
doc: A clock reading 0, with no task sleeping.

members.name: now
doc: The time the clock reads.

members.name: sleep
doc: Waits until the clock reads `span` later than it does now.

members.name: jump
doc: Moves to the earliest time a task sleeps until, unless that is past `end`, where it stops:
`.none` when it moved, else why the simulation ends.

items.name: never
doc: The time of no task sleeping.

items.name: Ended
doc: How a simulation's run ended: every task finished, the tasks left wait on events nothing will

doc: Runs `tasks`, borrows of `std.task.Async` frames, on `clock` until each finished, none can
go on, or the clock has moved `limit` past where it read: one ready task at a time, the
next chosen by the case's choices, the clock moved to the earliest time a task sleeps until
whenever none is ready.

members.name: ready
members.signature: ready := (done: bool, due: bool, waiting: &?std.task.Wait) -> bool

record of its caller's frame and of where it returns to at its frame pointer. A runtime's
handler of traps writes one before ending the program.

doc: The program's table, which the compiler defines.

items.name: depth
doc: The most frames a backtrace names: past them, the chain is taken to be broken.

doc: The address of the code of `f`.

doc: The function whose code holds `address`: the one starting last at or before it.

doc: The origin of index `index`.

doc: What the program's table says of a trap site: what it says, where that is known when
compiling, and where it is written.
